findings.location: Section-wide Refinement thread — cumulative-harm conflict absent
findings.claim_text: The section never raises whether repeated 'mild/moderate' laboratory procedures produce measurable long-term cumulative harm; the Refinement discussion treats severity as per-procedure only.
findings.issue: Conflict [3] fully suppressed: Wegener2021 (15-yr NHP blood-marker dataset finds NO cumulative harm) and Bateson2015 (telomere attrition as cumulative-severity biomarker predicting harm conventional markers miss) are BOTH uncited and the cumulative-harm question is nowhere in the text.
findings.evidence: Wegener2021 verbatim: '...did not provide support for the notion of long-term, cumulative effects on the monkeys' healthiness and well-being.' Bateson2015 verbatim: 'I propose that telomere attrition... provides a molecular measure of cumulative experience that could be used to assess the welfare impact... of experimental procedures.'
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence in the Refinement/severity paragraph noting the open dispute: repeated 'mild' procedures may impose cumulative damage conventional markers miss (Bateson2015), whereas a long NHP dataset detects none (Wegener2021) — a gap better-reported severity data would help resolve.

findings.claim_text: "severity assessment remains largely subjective with evidence-based methods scarce {cite:p}`Leenaars2019a`, and the regulatory severity categories are widely judged too underspecified to assign consistently {cite:p}`Smith2018, DeVleeschauwer2023`"
findings.issue: Conflict [6] one-sided: only the pessimistic 'too subjective/underspecified' side is given. Manthey2021 (the countervailing side) is omitted — an in-training exercise significantly improved personnel's ability to recognise and grade stress severity, showing reliability is partly trainable.
findings.evidence: Manthey2021 verbatim: 'The results were assessed comparatively and showed a significant increase in performance in all categories (p<0.001)' (a minority still could not distinguish healthy from stressed animals). Smith2018 verbatim: 'The examples of severity classification given in Annex VIII are limited in number, and have little descriptive power to aid assignment.'
findings.suggested_fix: Cite Manthey2021 and hedge: severity judgement is subjective and the categories under-specified (Smith2018, Leenaars2019a), yet targeted training measurably improves grading reliability (Manthey2021), even if residual subjectivity remains.

findings.location: '3Rs as a moral contract' (sentience expansion) and Replacement framing
findings.claim_text: "the recognition of sentience keeps expanding — to cephalopods on high-confidence evidence {cite:p}`Schnell2026`"
findings.issue: Conflict [11] one-sided: Schnell2026 (strong evidence of cephalopod sentience) is cited, but CrespiAbril2023 — which notes invertebrates' presumed non-sentience is exactly what makes them favoured 'replacement' models — is omitted. Expanding sentience undercuts the 'invertebrates = low-cost replacement' logic the review elsewhere leans on.
findings.evidence: CrespiAbril2023 verbatim: invertebrates' presumed non-sentience 'favours them as replacement models'; proposes a broadened 5Rs. Schnell2026 verbatim: 'There is strong evidence of sentience in octopuses and cuttlefish... six of eight criteria.'
findings.suggested_fix: Add CrespiAbril2023: note the tension that invertebrates are treated as ethically cheap 'replacement' models precisely because assumed non-sentient (CrespiAbril2023), an assumption the sentience evidence (Schnell2026) is steadily eroding.

findings.location: 'Is Refinement overtaking Replacement?' — reliability of welfare score-sheets
findings.claim_text: Severity-scoring discussion cites only validated grimace scales (Evangelista2021) plus the 'subjective/scarce' framing; the reliability of routine score-sheets to predict outcomes is not engaged.
findings.issue: Conflict [12] fully suppressed: Krueger2023 (standard score-sheet parameters insufficient to predict death in a rat cirrhosis model) and Moller2018 (a simple evidence-based severity classification is valid) are BOTH uncited, so the disagreement over how reliably simple welfare scores capture severity is absent.
findings.evidence: Krueger2023 verbatim: humane endpoint had to be re-derived ('scores exceeding 20') because standard parameters under-predicted death. Moller2018 verbatim: kindling paradigm classifiable as 'moderate severity based on a longer-lasting mild impact.'
findings.suggested_fix: Add both: routine score-sheets can fail to predict mortality and need model-specific re-calibration (Krueger2023), even as comprehensive evidence-based analyses can validly assign severity in other models (Moller2018).

findings.claim_text: "severity assessment remains largely subjective with evidence-based methods scarce {cite:p}`Leenaars2019a`"
findings.issue: The claim faithfully quotes Leenaars2019a, but the same package contains numerous validated/emerging evidence-based severity tools (TappeTheodor2022 — replicated; Reiber2023; Morton2023; Talbot2023; Leitner2026). Presenting only 'scarce' understates the maturing tool base.
findings.evidence: TappeTheodor2022 (replicated): 'The WWHow concept integrates intra-operative characteristics for predicting the maximum expected severity of surgical procedures.' Reiber2023: bioinformatics composite schemes 'confirmed... for evidence-based comparative severity assessment.'
findings.suggested_fix: Hedge: 'robust, cross-model-validated methods remain scarce, though a growing set of evidence-based severity tools is being developed and validated {cite:p}`TappeTheodor2022, Reiber2023`.'

findings.claim_text: "Support is real but conditional and sensitive to species and purpose, averaging no better than ambivalence in structured consultations {cite:p}`Brunt2021b`"
findings.issue: The section uses Brunt2021b only for the 'ambivalence' reading; the conflict [4] facet — that specific high-benefit scenarios drew HIGHER-than-typical support (the 'more supportive than commonly assumed' side vs Joffe2016) — is dropped. Both papers are cited so the conflict is not fully suppressed, but the framing is one-directional.
findings.evidence: Brunt2021b: scenarios 'all exhibited higher levels of support than what is typically reported for animal research'; overall mean 4.5/7 (ambivalence). Joffe2016: 'Expectations for AR are much higher than empirical data show to have been achieved.'
findings.suggested_fix: Add the counter-facet: while overall attitudes average ambivalent, specific high-benefit scenarios drew higher-than-typical support (Brunt2021b), complicating the 'fragile support' reading drawn from Joffe2016.

findings.location: 'A framework honoured in the breach' — checklist enforcement
findings.claim_text: "A checklist mandated at submission has been associated with more complete reporting {cite:p}`Han2017`, whereas the mere publication of reporting guidelines left adherence unchanged or even lower {cite:p}`Liu2021`"
findings.issue: The section presents mandated checklists favourably, but the citemap contains Macleod2019b (the IICARus randomised trial), whose null result — a mandated ARRIVE checklist at peer review did NOT improve compliance — nuances the 'mandating works' claim. (Macleod2019b has no section_03 finding, so this is a caveat rather than a coverage SHOULD_CITE.)
findings.evidence: Han2017 and Macleod2019b both in citemap; the mandated-checklist evidence is mixed (association in Han2017 vs a null RCT in Macleod2019b/IICARus).
findings.suggested_fix: Soften: 'mandating a checklist at submission has been associated with more complete reporting {cite:p}`Han2017`, though a randomised trial of enforced checklist review found no improvement {cite:p}`Macleod2019b` — enforcement helps but is not sufficient.'

findings.location: 'A framework honoured in the breach' (para after fig-sec3-3rs-underreporting)
findings.claim_text: "...mouse papers averaging zero of ten possible items {cite:p}`Taylor2010`; ... sample-size estimation reported in 1.0% {cite:p}`Park2023`; ... adherence to the ARRIVE 2.0 essentials at 42% {cite:p}`Ding2022`; ... a 2.35% data-sharing response rate {cite:p}`Ratajczak2024`. These are replicated findings, not outliers..."
findings.issue: Cross-paper synthesis pools four different metrics (a 10-item 3Rs score, sample-size reporting, ARRIVE-essentials adherence, data-sharing response rate) with different denominators as 'the same low rates.' Directionally sound (text notes 'across specialties, methods, and decades'), but the metrics are not commensurable point-for-point; 42% is not a low single-digit rate like the others.
findings.evidence: Each statistic measures a distinct reporting item; ARRIVE-essentials adherence (42%) differs in kind from single-digit sample-size/analgesia rates.
findings.suggested_fix: Minor wording: 'consistently low across distinct reporting metrics' rather than implying a single comparable rate.

findings.claim_text: "male-only study designs generate surpluses of unused female animals... {cite:p}`Onuma2026`"
findings.issue: Package contains two distinct papers whose cite_keys differ only by case: Onuma2026 (10.1002/ame2.70182, correctly cited here) and ONUMA2026 (10.1292/jvms.25-0455, uncited vet-student compassion study). Case-insensitive BibTeX/MyST tooling can collide or mis-resolve these.
findings.suggested_fix: Rename one key (e.g. ONUMA2026 -> Onuma2026b) to remove the case-only collision before bibliography build.
